title: JavaScript Memory Management Applied Check
description: Apply JavaScript memory management concepts by identifying leaks, choosing cleanup patterns, using weak collections appropriately, and reasoning about async and large data memory pressure.
author: DailyCoder

options.text: The global `logs` array can grow forever and retain full event objects
Arrays cannot store events
The function has no return statement, so it cannot use memory
`const` makes the array unreachable

questions.explanation: A long-lived array that grows without limits can retain more and more memory, especially if it stores large event objects.

options.text: Store a small value like `card.id` instead of the DOM node
Call `removeCard()` twice
Rename `removedCards` to `cards`
Wrap `card.remove()` in `String()`

questions.explanation: Storing the DOM node keeps it reachable after removal. Storing only an ID avoids retaining the detached node.

options.text: A function that calls `clearInterval(id)`
A function that calls `JSON.stringify(element)`
A function that creates another interval
No cleanup is possible for intervals

questions.explanation: The interval keeps running until it is cleared, and its callback retains `element`.

options.text: The anonymous function cannot easily be passed later to `removeEventListener()`
Click listeners never use memory
Arrow functions cannot access variables
`saveForm` automatically removes the listener

questions.explanation: To remove a listener, you need the same function reference that was used when adding it.

options.text: The returned `search` function closes over `users`
`filter()` always leaks memory
String methods prevent garbage collection
The array is converted to a primitive

questions.explanation: The returned function retains the outer `users` variable, so the passed list remains reachable while the function is reachable.

questions.prompt: Which option is best for metadata associated with DOM elements that should not keep removed elements alive?

options.text: `WeakMap` keyed by element objects
A module-level `Map` that never deletes entries
A global array of every element ever seen
A string made by joining all element HTML

questions.explanation: A `WeakMap` can associate metadata with object keys without strongly retaining those keys.

options.text: The user object is still retained as a key in `metadata`
The user object is guaranteed to be collected immediately
The map deletes the entry automatically
Only the string `admin` is retained

questions.explanation: A regular `Map` strongly references keys, so setting the local variable to `null` is not enough.

questions.prompt: Which approach handles a fetch that may outlive the current UI?

options.text: Use `AbortController` and abort during cleanup when possible
Ignore all errors forever
Store every response globally
Use `setInterval()` around the request

questions.explanation: `AbortController` lets supported APIs such as `fetch` cancel work that is no longer needed.

questions.prompt: What does `Promise.race()` timeout logic not do by itself?

options.text: It does not automatically stop the slower underlying operation
It does not settle promises
It cannot reject
It deletes every pending variable

questions.explanation: `Promise.race()` chooses the first settled result, but cancellation requires support from the underlying operation.

questions.prompt: A cache stores API results in a `Map` and memory grows as more IDs are loaded. What is the most practical first improvement?

options.text: Add an eviction strategy such as a size limit
Make the map global so it is easier to find
Replace every object with a DOM node
Never read from the cache

questions.explanation: A bounded cache keeps performance benefits while preventing unlimited growth.

questions.prompt: Which debugging workflow is most useful for suspected leaks?

options.text: Repeat the action, take heap snapshots before and after cleanup, and inspect retaining paths
Look only at one random number in the console
Assume all memory growth is a leak
Delete unrelated source files

questions.explanation: Memory debugging is evidence-driven: reproduce growth, compare snapshots, and find what retains old objects.

options.text: It may load all responses into memory at once
`Promise.all()` prevents arrays from being created
`fetch` returns only booleans
JSON responses are never stored in memory

questions.explanation: Running many requests and parsing all JSON results concurrently can hold many large values in memory at the same time.

questions.prompt: What should code do when `WeakRef#deref()` returns `undefined`?

options.text: Treat the object as unavailable and recreate or skip it as appropriate
Assume the object is definitely still alive
Call properties on `undefined`
Disable garbage collection

questions.explanation: A weakly referenced object may have been collected, so code must handle `undefined` safely.

questions.prompt: Which code shape makes cleanup easiest?

options.text: A setup function that returns a cleanup function
A setup function that hides all timer IDs
A global array of anonymous callbacks
A listener created without any function reference

questions.explanation: Returning cleanup from setup keeps lifecycle responsibilities explicit and testable.

questions.prompt: A heap snapshot shows a removed element retained by `window -> appState -> selectedCard -> element`. What should you investigate first?

options.text: Why `appState.selectedCard` still references the removed element
Whether CSS colors are too bright
Whether the element's text is uppercase
Whether `console.log` is installed

questions.explanation: The retaining path points to the reference chain keeping the element alive, so the fix should target that ownership path.
